About

AI benchmarks can feel like witchcraft. Witchbench follows the ingredients: which benchmarks OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google choose to highlight when releasing coding-capable models in 2026, and which they evaluate in their model cards. We track attention, with two checks and a trail back to the archived evidence. Created by Dmitry Lyalin, this independent project welcomes corrections, contributions, and disagreement through GitHub.

How the checks work

Blog: launch prose discusses the release model’s performance or limitations on a named benchmark. A name in a table, caption, citation, or setup note alone does not qualify.

Card: the card reports a numerical evaluation for the release model. References to other models and table-of-contents entries do not qualify. The site and CSV contain coverage flags only; original source documents retain their full content.

Rows rank by distinct release events with either check; an event with both checks counts once. Benchmark versions stay separate. Grouped models are one announcement event, and preview and general releases remain separate. The chart shows monthly usage among matching events. A blank means no qualifying finding in this snapshot; a missing card is labeled separately.

This MVP uses deterministic text rules with source-linked evidence. It is open to correction and has not received a full independent manual audit. Chart text is extracted from archived images; OCR and PDF extraction can still miss evidence. The September 29, 2026 snapshot covers the supplied research set; future months are not populated.

Sources, credit, and rights

Every source has a retrieval timestamp, original URL, and SHA-256 checksum in the source archive. Original HTML and PDFs are preserved alongside extracted text. These are local research snapshots, not guarantees about the current live pages.
